newsitem.title: UK: Educating doctors could improve organ donation.
newsitem.headline: Educating doctors could improve organ donation.

text.p: A programme to educate emergency room doctors and other health professionals on how to deal with bereaved relatives could help bring in more organs for transplants, an expert said on Thursday.

Simple counselling techniques could be used to gently persuade grieving relatives to allow organs from their loved ones to save someone else's life, Robert Johnson, head of the British Transplantation Society, told a conference.
Johnson told the conference at the Royal Society of Medicine in London that about 2,000 transplants were done in Britain each year, but the waiting list for organs was 6,000 long and growing.
The latter figure was close to 50,000 in the United States.
He said the delays could be slashed if more people would agree to donate their organs after death, and if relatives could be persuaded to agree.

One problem is that organs need to be removed and transplanted as soon as possible after death. This often means confronting, for example, a couple who have just been stunned by news their teenaged son has died in an automobile accident.
"A lot of donor relatives are of course very angry," Johnson told Reuters in an interview during the conference. "People in intensive care units haven't been taught to deal with these things."

The European Donor Hospital Education Programme (EDHEP) was doing just this. It was being tested in Liverpool and Manchester in northwest England and had already increased organ donations by 30 percent.
"It's really been very, very popular with those who do the course," Johnson said.

Another programme using professional organ scouts had worked in Spain and could be used elsewhere in Europe, he said. Such coordinators were put in every general hospital in Spain and had greatly increased the rate of donations.
"We are moving towards the idea of coordination," he said.
Doctors could also eliminate wastage by better matching organs to recipients and screening out poor-prospect recipients like those with chronic heart disease, he said.
